blocks.text: Performance strategy / Program design
Delivery Lead Bootcamp
A clearer starting point for a complex role.

As the managed services ERP systems practice grew, more people entered Delivery Lead roles. Leadership acted early: varied experience and a few warning signs suggested uneven preparation before larger engagements.
THE PROGRAM THROUGHLINE
Follow the work.
Initiate Set expectations and governance
Deliver Lead operations and risk
Renew Show value at renewal
MY ROLE
I led the design workstream and built the program blueprint.
I scheduled stakeholder meetings, guided session workstreams, and oversaw delivery. The program was designed and delivered with the broader team.
Audience ranged from Senior Associates through Directors.
How I framed it.

Looking back, this was a readiness risk, not a documented decline. The map clarified expectations; simulations and peers supported practice. Training alone was not enough. I proposed coaching afterward.
Three days. One engagement arc.
Leaders considered urgent topics first. I advocated for the engagement lifecycle so each day built toward the capstone. Leadership agreed; I think the sequence felt more cohesive.
Illustrative agenda · adapted session titles
DAY 01 Launch the engagement Program welcome Cohort connections Starting a client engagement Working across cultures
DAY 02 Lead the delivery AI in delivery decisions AI judgment lab Commercial tradeoffs Service operations
DAY 03 Close and renew Quality signals and risk Closing and continuing the work Final case challenge · 2 hours
Sessions ran 45–90 minutes, longer for priority topics. After lunch: protected work time.
What we wanted Delivery Leads to do.
These were program aims. They are not claims of measured performance gains.
Outcome ownership
Lead the engagement
Clarify ownership and take responsibility for delivery decisions.
PRACTICE Launch planning and team scenarios
Business Context & Responsible Delivery
Run the business
Weigh risk, quality, finances, and client value in delivery decisions.
PRACTICE Operational scenarios and capstone
AI-Native Delivery
Deliver through AI
Use AI-assisted inputs with human judgment and accountability.
PRACTICE AI judgment lab and capstone
Across all three, cultural agility, a service mindset, and peer learning shaped the practice.
The capstone put those decisions together.
Just before the capstone, teams met a fictional client: 90 minutes for decisions, then 30 for presentations and feedback.
DECISION AREAS Launch · Recovery · Finances · Quality · Renewal · AI use
A decision under pressure.
When ticket handoffs stall resolution, who owns recovery, and when should the Delivery Lead escalate?
This newly written RAID (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies) excerpt shows the kind of decision evidence an activity could surface. It is not an original participant artifact.
RISK OR ISSUE
Unclear ticket handoffs delay resolution and obscure accountability.
OWNER & NEXT ACTION
The Delivery Lead assigns a handoff owner, reviews open work, and confirms the recovery path with the client contact.
ESCALATION TRIGGER
Escalate through agreed governance if ownership stays unresolved or the recovery plan risks a client commitment.
WHY
One named owner restores accountability before speed. The trigger keeps the client commitment visible.
A strong entry shows the action and the reasoning: why this owner, why this trigger.
“We would validate sustained performance with the client before calling the improvement durable.”
What we heard. What I'd change next time.

Respondents reported applicable skills, rated the program highly, and felt confident they understood the Delivery Lead role. Launch and cross-cultural sessions were especially valued; leadership feedback was positive.
After observing the Bootcamp, I proposed more preparation, longer simulations, lighter content, stronger behavior assessment, capstone evidence criteria, and follow-up coaching.

The available account does not include survey response counts, capstone scores, or post-program delivery measures. Reported confidence and value do not establish improved job performance. The next-iteration items above were proposals.
